reason: KG-embedding training system is only systems-adjacent and the scout found no released implementation, which violates the hard requirement.
Quantized LLM serving kernels with a named AE repo fit one 24 GB GPU once 4-bit weights shrink the model; H100-tuned numbers mean Ampere retuning is itself a plausible improvement hypothesis.
Single-GPU DNN compiler is systems-adjacent, but the artifact ships as a Docker image on an unresponsive Zenodo record and would need an LLVM-16 + PipLib user-space rebuild.
GPU multitasking is a great single-A5000 topic, but nothing is public yet — no abstract, no preprint, no artifact — so it cannot be built upon.

CPU/SIMD lossless float compression with a clean public repo and DuckDB integration runs trivially here; compression-scheme variants and new datasets are easy testable hypotheses, though it is storage-adjacent rather than OS resource management.

GPU spatial multiplexing and interference estimation is squarely OS resource management, but MIG is unavailable on an A5000 so sharing must fall back to MPS/streams and the cluster placement arm needs simulation.
Single-node C++/Python vector index with a latency cost model builds here and the cost model is a clear knob to improve; NUMA-aware parallelism cannot be studied on one NUMA node.
Headline experiments need root for modprobe/mount of in-kernel file systems; only a much weaker FUSE-only study survives, and the contribution is bug-finding rather than resource management.
ML inside a query optimizer is the weakest topic fit and there is no public artifact from the industrial authors.

Request migration and scheduling for LLM serving is a textbook OS scheduling problem with a linked artifact and many policy knobs; the catch is that it needs multiple instances, so a scale-down to small models or the bundled simulator is required.
The A5000 has the RT cores needed to reproduce it, but mapping query operators onto OptiX is a database-acceleration result with little OS resource-management content.

LSM file placement across a storage hierarchy under RocksDB is core storage systems with a public repo, but the single NVMe tier means device classes must be emulated with cgroups or loopback, weakening the headline claim.

Serverless resource-allocation policy whose Zenodo artifact bundles the full measured performance dataset, so the policy search can be re-run and improved offline; only fresh cloud measurements are out of reach.
Multicore transaction scheduling fits the hardware well but no public artifact was found, so it would have to be reimplemented from scratch.
Graph processing on tensor runtimes is only loosely a systems-resource problem and no repo was located.

Multicore user-space CSV parsing runs perfectly on 16 cores with an evaluation repo linked, but it is a data-processing kernel rather than OS resource management and the improvable surface is mostly vectorization micro-tuning.
CLIP/Whisper-class models fit one GPU and the repo is linked, but scheduling ML inference inside relational operators is a query-processing contribution with modest OS relevance.

Accuracy-scaling inference serving is a genuine scheduling/resource-allocation problem with trace-driven evaluation, but it targets a heterogeneous cluster so a single-GPU or simulated scale-down is mandatory.

A vLLM plug-in explicitly designed for memory-constrained devices, so a 24 GB GPU is the intended target and no scale-down is needed; batching/scheduling knobs for test-time scaling give clear hypotheses.
The placement policy is simulator-friendly, but there is no public artifact and the evaluation depends on datacenter power/thermal telemetry we cannot obtain.

Pure user-space trace transformation is easy to run and directly reusable methodology, but validation originally replays against real servers so on one host it degrades to a loopback experiment at reduced load.

Page-level migration for tiered storage is a real resource-management policy with a linked repo and obvious policy-swap experiments, but our single NVMe tier forces emulated tiers or trace-only evaluation.
Open source and user-space buildable, but the primary backend is AMD CDNA matrix cores so NVIDIA Ampere support is unproven, and a user-space LLVM/MLIR build is a heavy 10-week tax.
The design is evaluated entirely on a user-space simulator with improvable mapping and GC policies, but the repo link is an unresponsive institutional host and the release could not be confirmed.
Only the CPU-only planner and cost model are runnable here; without a heterogeneous multi-GPU cluster any improvement must be argued from planner search quality alone.

A storage prefetch policy evaluated purely by replaying public block traces with an explicit artifact repo — no root, no special hardware, and prefetch/clustering heuristics are an obvious space of testable policy swaps.
Single-node PostgreSQL with small models is easy to run, but a learned query-plan selector is the anchor case for weak OS-course topic fit.
Ordinary Tensor Core kernels run on Ampere and the Microsoft repo is public; the 70B accuracy runs must move to 7-8B models, which is exactly the kind of scale-down the note calls plausible.
Clean CPU-only Python artifact that runs effortlessly, but multi-query reuse across ML pipeline re-executions is a data-systems optimization with little OS content.
Concurrent in-memory B-tree in C++ scales naturally to 32 threads with a public repo; the point-versus-range tradeoff knob is a ready-made testable hypothesis.

Distinguished-artifact quality release with clean single-machine metrics (verification time, SMT queries), but it is verification tooling rather than a resource-management system and the proof corpus is CPU-hours-heavy.
Single-host JVM stream-engine throughput study with an artifact statement; needs a conda JDK and the improvable claim is operator-level throughput rather than a systems policy.

The federation can be simulated on one GPU with small models, but the headline results depend on mobile NPUs we lack and the core contribution is a training-algorithm idea more than systems resource management.
GC-plus-defragmentation in a user-space dedup store is exactly the kind of storage policy this course wants, but the AE repo currently 404s and the backup datasets are large against 257 GB free.
Pure user-space Python that runs anywhere, but AutoML pipeline selection is an ML-workflow contribution rather than a systems-resource one.
Compiler testing is CPU-only and rootless, but it is a PL bug-finding tool with no public artifact — the two weakest axes combined.
CPU sparse-kernel tiling fits the 16-core box perfectly, but no official repo was found and sparse linear algebra is only marginally an OS topic.
Actively maintained open framework, but the collocate-versus-disaggregate placement contribution largely evaporates with a single 24 GB GPU, leaving only tiny LoRA policies.

Credit-based fair allocation evaluated by trace-driven simulation over production workloads with a public repo — no hardware dependency at all; part of the contribution is game-theoretic proofs, so the improvable surface is the allocation algorithm.
LSM knob tuning on RocksDB is a fine single-node storage project with plenty of tunable-heuristic headroom, but no artifact was located.
Single-GPU temporal-GNN training batching is runnable in principle, but no official repo was found and the topic is ML training rather than OS resource management.
CPU-only C++ compression on top of the well-maintained SZ3 repo (qoi branch); the main friction is tens of GB of scientific reference datasets and a fairly closed error-control result.
INT4 tensor cores exist on sm_86 so the mechanism would run, but no official repo was found and reimplementing mixed-precision W4Ax kernels in 10 weeks is unrealistic.
Workload-driven LSM compaction on RocksDB with a public repo: single-node, no root, and the compaction decision engine is an obvious space of policy swaps and new workloads.
Microsoft repo is public and medium XC benchmarks fit 24 GB, but the headline label sets do not fit and GPU-memory tricks for extreme classification are a narrow training-systems topic.
User-space checkpoint/restore of a process's live state is a classic OS mechanism, it is pure Python on one machine with no root, and the migration cost model invites policy improvements.
A cache admission/eviction policy inside RocksDB is an ideal topic and trivially runnable, but no repo was located so the hard requirement fails.
Buffer-pool replacement plus I/O parallelisation on NVMe is core caching and I/O management, needs no kernel changes, has a public repo, and eviction-policy variants are directly testable.
CPU-only model fuzzing runs easily and the code was upstreamed into P, but the paper's own artifact URL 404s and testing distributed-system models is far from OS resource management.
Domain-specific trajectory compression with no located repo — narrow topic and unbuildable as listed.
User-space CUDA-interception checkpoint/restore is a genuine OS mechanism demonstrable on one A5000 with a well-maintained repo; the risk is tight coupling to CUDA/driver versions against driver 535.
Solid user-space Rust/Python compiler with a clear performance objective, but ZK proving is memory- and time-hungry and the subject matter is cryptographic compilation rather than OS resources.

A pure single-GPU memory-versus-runtime tradeoff, but the work was upstreamed into PyTorch's default min-cut partitioner, so the baseline is now production code and any improvement must beat current PyTorch.
Learned cardinality estimation is the weakest topic fit for an OS course and no public repo was found.

Offloading dormant MoE experts to host DRAM is a GPU/host memory tiering problem that suits 24 GB GPU plus 125 GiB RAM, though the activation predictor adds offline training cost and the largest MoEs need scale-down.

The analysis tool itself is user-space, but it checks equivalence of distributed training graphs whose motivating bugs need multi-GPU runs, leaving a closed correctness result with little to extend here.
Learned filters inside a data-series index run on one machine with a public repo, but this is an indexing/ML-for-DB result rather than an OS resource-management one.

The artifact ships both datasets and model so the whole study is trace-driven on CPU or one GPU; a container image must be ported to conda, and failure prediction is a learned-component study rather than a resource policy.
Single-GPU W4A4 serving with an official lab repo and sm_86 INT4 support; kernels were tuned for A100/4090, so A5000 retuning is both a risk and a ready-made improvement hypothesis.
Batch-level partitioning under single-GPU memory pressure is precisely a one-GPU memory-management problem, with both Zenodo and GitHub artifacts and clear partitioning-policy variants.
Compiled decision trees run trivially on CPU with a public repo, but query performance prediction is an ML-for-DB contribution with limited OS relevance.

Contention-aware placement is a real scheduling topic with an Available+Functional+Reproduced artifact, but the multi-node Kubernetes Flink setup collapses to several TaskManagers under cgroup limits, weakening the story.
Only a static-analysis tool is public with no abstract; the end-to-end evaluation is on Uber production microservices and open microservice benchmarks assume Docker, which is unavailable.

CPU-only data-layout work on memory access patterns and auto-vectorization runs perfectly on 16 cores with a clean repo; layout/pruning variants give real headroom, but it is a data-structure contribution.

Removing KV-cache init and CUDA-graph capture cold-start stages is a single-GPU OS-style mechanism with a public repo; artifact completeness is unknown and CUDA-graph paths depend on the driver version.
Trains and runs entirely on one machine with a linked repo, but a learned query optimizer sits at the bottom of the os_fit scale for this course.

KV-cache-reuse-maximizing request reordering against a single-GPU vLLM with Llama-3-8B is exactly our hardware; the reordering algorithm is CPU-side and swapping in better orderings is a clean testable hypothesis.
Shared/nested parameter serving is a great memory-management topic, but the paper uses 70B-class models that do not fit and no code was found.
In-memory range filter for key-value stores in the SuRF/Rosetta line: user-space, single machine, public repo, and false-positive-versus-space tradeoffs are easy hypotheses.
A released evaluation testbed runs easily, but this is a measurement/comparison study of ML-for-DB representations with essentially no systems mechanism to improve.
The single-machine claim helps, but the 5-billion-edge experiments exceed our RAM and disk and the distributed arm is out of reach; graph mining is also only weakly an OS topic.
User-space C++ multicore engine that builds here, but as the note says the flavour is graph analytics rather than OS-level systems.
Learned-index construction with 32-thread concurrency experiments would fit the machine, but no artifact was found in search.
Decentralized task scheduling studied by simulation over public Google/Alibaba traces is explicitly allowed by scope; only the simulator path is usable since the k8s prototype needs a real cluster.
Pipelining schedules for dataflow DAGs is a legitimate user-space scheduling problem, but no repo was located.
Out-of-core training with I/O-efficient feature packing on one GPU plus NVMe matches this machine exactly, with a public repo and clear packing/prefetch knobs to vary.
Tiny pure-Python CPU workload that runs anywhere, but accelerating AutoML search by data subsetting has almost no OS-systems content.

Single-GPU Tensor Core kernels with an Available+Functional+Reproduced artifact and Ampere TCUs present; it is GPU kernel engineering rather than resource management, and newer-CUDA kernels may need a conda toolkit on driver 535.
Plain Java user-space sketch that runs in minutes on one core, but it is closer to an algorithms paper than a systems one and the CAIDA traces need a data-access agreement.

Far-memory management with a user-space runtime and no kernel changes is a strong memory-management topic with a public repo; the CloudLab far-memory backend must be replaced by a local loopback or second-process memory server.
